source.title: CodeCircuit: Toward Inferring LLM-Generated Code Correctness via Attribution Graphs
source.authors: Yi-Cheng He; Zheng-Yang Zhao; Kai Zhou; Bryan Dai; Jie Fu; Yonghui Yang

record.tranche_reason: The study uses attribution graphs and transcoder features as tools for code verification, but does not test whether neuron poles have one or two main jobs, whether explanations predict activations on held-out examples, or whether neurons alone suffice as circuit units.
record.gate_note: The paper reports CodeCircuit classifier performance in Tables 1 and 2 and a complexity trend in Figure 3. These evaluate the paper's own graph-based verifier, which uses a trained GBDT and transcoder-based graphs; they do not directly measure the neuron-level claims. The separate causal intervention in Table 3 is recorded under fits_no_version because it acts on a transcoder feature, not a neuron.
record.test_reason: The study uses transcoder-based attribution graphs (with error nodes) as a tool to build a code-correctness verifier for Gemma-2-2B-IT and reports its own verifier's performance. It measures no neuron-level interpretability shares, explanation accuracy, or neuron-only circuit sufficiency, so it bears on none of V1–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that attribution-graph topology from transcoder features predicts line-level code correctness across Python, Java and C++ better than black-box and gray-box baselines, and transfers across languages. They also claim that interventions on graph features can causally fix errors. They frame the method as an aid to, not a replacement for, human review and testing.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a trained GemmaScope transcoder replacement model, explicit error nodes, and a trained GBDT verifier; it does not construct graphs from neurons alone.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that verifier performance changes with programming language, train/test language transfer, and task complexity.

fits_no_version.finding: In one binary-search case, zeroing a mid-layer transcoder feature labelled 'greedy matching' changed 'high = mid' to 'high = mid - 1'. The resulting code was functionally correct.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Targeted interventions on transcoder features found by attribution graphs can correct individual code-generation errors.

record.problems: The reported causal intervention is a single case study, with no uncertainty estimate stated. The attribution graphs rely on trained transcoders and include error nodes, so they do not establish neuron-only sufficiency.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 1 and 2 report the performance of the study's own trained CodeCircuit verifier against other methods, and Figure 3 reports its complexity trend. These are verifier-method results rather than direct measurements of the neuron-level claims, so they were not extracted as rows.

untested.parts: All: neuron-pole job shares in Qwen3-32B.

record.verdict_notes: Gemma-2-2B-IT only. Correctness labels come from GPT-4o. The paper cites Bills et al. 2023, an original source, only in related work. The study never reports interpretability rates of neurons or features.

versions.untested_parts: Neuron-pole job shares and the proportion not understood.
Neuron-pole interpretability across model families, sizes, dense or mixture-of-experts architectures, and scales up to trillions of parameters.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Architecture, regularization, tool quality, and the claimed interpretability shares for InceptionV1-sized vision models.

Whether attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons explain behavior without trained replacement models or reconstruction-error terms. The paper instead uses trained transcoders and includes error nodes.
Whether explanations fitting activating examples fail to predict where neurons fire.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B-IT
rows.operation_detail: Suppressed a transcoder feature described as a greedy-matching feature by zeroing its activation during generation.
rows.value: After intervention: high = mid - 1; the paper states the resulting solution was functionally correct.
rows.note: This is a single qualitative case study. The intervened unit is a transcoder feature, not a neuron.
rows.check: This is a single qualitative case of suppressing a transcoder feature, not a neuron. It shows the paper's method working, not a version of the claim. The link to 'none' is right; 'observed' only describes the intervention's own success and says nothing about any version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
